nodes.title: TAXONOMY
nodes.body:
Common Name:  Naked goby
Scientific Name:  Gobiosoma bosci

nodes.title: Classification
nodes.body:
Phylum:  Chordata
	Class:  Actinopterygii
	Order:  Perciformes
	Family:  Gobiidae

Synonyms: Gobiosoma bosci (Lacepède, 1800) (misspelling)

Other Common Names:  gobio desnudo

Note:	Reference for Scientific Name (Lacepede 1800).
	Reference for Classification (1914).
	Revision date should be checked.
Superclass: Osteichthyes

nodes.title: VALUE & STATUS
nodes.body:
Commercial:  None
Recreational:  None
Ecological:  Because it is common or abundant in estuarine and oligohaline hard bottom habitats, the naked goby is of ecological importance. It is an abundant primary and secondary consumer and prey for a variety of invertebrates and fishes (163).  Dovel (1971) and Shenker et al. (1983) found that as the numerically dominant ichthyoplankton in Chesapeake Bay, the naked goby may potentially be a valuable forage source for fish and other planktonic predators.  As adults they are abundant members of the oyster reef community.
Indicator:  None known

nodes.title: GEOGRAPHIC RANGE
nodes.body:
Overall:  The naked goby is found in estuarine waters from Long Island Sound to Campeche, Mexico (2465; 2469).
Within Study Area:  The naked goby is found throughout the Indian River Lagoon in marginal wetlands, tidal creeks, canals, tributaries, and in association with spoil islands (887; 848; 2320; 2215).
Mobility and Migration:
Larvae: larval forms of the naked goby move upstream into fresher water in the Chesapeake Bay region before returning to the adult oyster reef habitat to settle (2469).
Adult: adults appear to be sedentary with restricted movements associated with territories within oyster reef habitat (2466).
Life Mode:  The naked goby associates with benthic structures, commonly settling in oyster reefs as juvenile and adults (2461; 2466).  The eggs are laid in oyster shells and hatch into planktonic larvae that move into lower salinity waters (2461; 2469).

nodes.title: Habitat Type
nodes.body:
The adult naked goby is generally associated with oyster bars or reefs or other hard substrate in areas where salinities are generally less than 22 ppt (2356; 2321).  This goby can also be found in grassy areas and marsh ponds (312; 378).  Immediately after hatching, larvae are found in the plankton and may migrate "upstream" to areas of even lower salinity (2321; 2469).  Presettlement "demersal" larvae are found in the water column over juvenile settlement habitat which is the same oyster habitat as the adults (2458, 1991).
Substrate:  Oyster bars and reefs are the principle substrate along with other shell and hard substrates, including wood debris and fouling communities (1836; 2461).

nodes.title: Physical/chemical
nodes.body:
Salinity: In the southeastern U.S., this goby is found in brackish waters with salinities ranging from 0 to 33 ppt (664; 1812; 885). They are much more abundant in lower salinity areas typically associated with freshwater input (2466).
Temperature: temperatures range from 11 to 32.5 C (664; 885).

nodes.title: REPRODUCTION
nodes.body:
Reproductive Mode:  The naked goby is oviparous, gonochoristic, sexually dimorphic, and polygamous within a social hierarchy; eggs are fertilized externally in an oyster shell nest and guarded by the dominant breeding males (1915; 2461; 2466; 2469).
Mating/Spawning: Male naked gobies defend a nest site in an oyster shell.  They select the appropriate shell that allows access and defensibility (2460).  They produce sounds during territorial defense and to attract a mate (2466).  The ripe female is lead to the oyster shell selected by the male as a nest (2466).  Both male and female enter the shell for about 2-3 hrs during mating after which the female leaves the site (2466).  Dahlberg and Conyers (1973) found that a single male may mate with multiple females at different times. Egg counts of 330 to 2,000 were common although nests may contain up to 9,000 eggs.  These large nests frequently contain eggs at various stages of development (2461).  The males guard and fan the eggs until they hatch in 4-5 days (Saksena and Joseph (1972).  Spawning season in Mississippi begins in April and continues through October in Mississippi and Tampa Bay (664, 2462).  High summer maximum temperatures may suppress spawning as it does for G. robustum in Tampa Bay (2470).
Fecundity: The information on fecundity is limited, but Dahlberg and Conyers (1973) found between 701 and 1,382 eggs in the ovaries of 3 naked gobies collected in Georgia.

nodes.title: Length Range
nodes.body:
Egg:  The unfertilized egg of the naked goby is an opaque yellow sphere approximately 0.5 mm in diameter (2359), but may be as large as 0.72 mm (2461).  After fertilization, the elliptical egg, measuring 1.2-1.4 mm along the major axis and 0.5-0.7 mm along the minor, is demersal and attached by fibrous bundles (2359, 2321).  Eggs hatch in 4-5 days at 24 to 28 C (2321).
Larvae:  Newly hatched naked gobies are between 2.0 and 2.6 mm and have a conspicuous swim bladder (2359, 2321).  These larvae are planktonic and disperse throughout the water column (Nero 1977).  The size range of planktonic larvae is from 2 to 12 mm TL however the abundance of larvae in the water column declines rapidly above 8 mm.  Larvae above 8 mm become "demersal larvae" (2458).  Demersal larvae aggregate in shoals within 0.5 m of the substrate, usually above oyster bars, in groups of 2-3 up to several hundred individuals.  Demersal larvae range in size from 7 to 11 mm TL.  Upon collection, larger demersal larvae will settle on their pelvic fins in typical goby fashion and within a day become pigmented and indistinguishable from small juveniles (2458, 1991).  Settlement of larvae usually occurs at 9-12 mm TL (2458).
Juvenile:  After settlement, metamorphosis occurs rapidly with pigment developing in the dorsal area within 24 hrs (2459).  Juveniles may grow to 18 mm during their first summer of life (2358).
Adult:  Maturity is reached between 25 and 30 mm (2358), however males typically reach a larger size with the largest male reaching 50 mm and the largest female reaching only 37 mm (2461).  Males also tend to have darker body coloration (1915).  The sexes are distinguishable by the shape of their genital papilla with the male's being triangular and compressed while the female's is conical and fleshy (2464).

nodes.title: FOOD HABITS
nodes.body: Hildebrand and Schroeder (1928) found that naked gobies in Chesapeake Bay eat Gammarus amphipods, other small crustaceans, annelids, small fish and fish eggs.

nodes.title: ECOLOGICAL INTERACTIONS
nodes.body: Because it is common or abundant in estuarine and oligohaline hard bottom habitats, the naked goby is of ecological importance. It is an abundant primary and secondary consumer and prey for a variety of invertebrates and fishes (163).  Dovel (1971) and Shenker et al. (1983) found that as the numerically dominant ichthyoplankton in Chesapeake Bay, the naked goby may potentially be a valuable forage source for other fish species.  As adults they are abundant members of the oyster reef community.

sections.heading: TAXONOMY
sections.content:
Common Name:  Naked goby
Scientific Name:  Gobiosoma bosci

sections.heading: Classification
sections.content:
Phylum:  Chordata
	Class:  Actinopterygii
	Order:  Perciformes
	Family:  Gobiidae

Synonyms: Gobiosoma bosci (Lacepède, 1800) (misspelling)

Other Common Names:  gobio desnudo

Note:	Reference for Scientific Name (Lacepede 1800).
	Reference for Classification (1914).
	Revision date should be checked.
Superclass: Osteichthyes

sections.heading: VALUE & STATUS
sections.content:
Commercial:  None
Recreational:  None
Ecological:  Because it is common or abundant in estuarine and oligohaline hard bottom habitats, the naked goby is of ecological importance. It is an abundant primary and secondary consumer and prey for a variety of invertebrates and fishes (163).  Dovel (1971) and Shenker et al. (1983) found that as the numerically dominant ichthyoplankton in Chesapeake Bay, the naked goby may potentially be a valuable forage source for fish and other planktonic predators.  As adults they are abundant members of the oyster reef community.
Indicator:  None known

sections.heading: GEOGRAPHIC RANGE
sections.content:
Overall:  The naked goby is found in estuarine waters from Long Island Sound to Campeche, Mexico (2465; 2469).
Within Study Area:  The naked goby is found throughout the Indian River Lagoon in marginal wetlands, tidal creeks, canals, tributaries, and in association with spoil islands (887; 848; 2320; 2215).
Mobility and Migration:
Larvae: larval forms of the naked goby move upstream into fresher water in the Chesapeake Bay region before returning to the adult oyster reef habitat to settle (2469).
Adult: adults appear to be sedentary with restricted movements associated with territories within oyster reef habitat (2466).
Life Mode:  The naked goby associates with benthic structures, commonly settling in oyster reefs as juvenile and adults (2461; 2466).  The eggs are laid in oyster shells and hatch into planktonic larvae that move into lower salinity waters (2461; 2469).

sections.heading: Habitat Type
sections.content:
The adult naked goby is generally associated with oyster bars or reefs or other hard substrate in areas where salinities are generally less than 22 ppt (2356; 2321).  This goby can also be found in grassy areas and marsh ponds (312; 378).  Immediately after hatching, larvae are found in the plankton and may migrate "upstream" to areas of even lower salinity (2321; 2469).  Presettlement "demersal" larvae are found in the water column over juvenile settlement habitat which is the same oyster habitat as the adults (2458, 1991).
Substrate:  Oyster bars and reefs are the principle substrate along with other shell and hard substrates, including wood debris and fouling communities (1836; 2461).

sections.heading: Physical/chemical
sections.content:
Salinity: In the southeastern U.S., this goby is found in brackish waters with salinities ranging from 0 to 33 ppt (664; 1812; 885). They are much more abundant in lower salinity areas typically associated with freshwater input (2466).
Temperature: temperatures range from 11 to 32.5 C (664; 885).

sections.heading: REPRODUCTION
sections.content:
Reproductive Mode:  The naked goby is oviparous, gonochoristic, sexually dimorphic, and polygamous within a social hierarchy; eggs are fertilized externally in an oyster shell nest and guarded by the dominant breeding males (1915; 2461; 2466; 2469).
Mating/Spawning: Male naked gobies defend a nest site in an oyster shell.  They select the appropriate shell that allows access and defensibility (2460).  They produce sounds during territorial defense and to attract a mate (2466).  The ripe female is lead to the oyster shell selected by the male as a nest (2466).  Both male and female enter the shell for about 2-3 hrs during mating after which the female leaves the site (2466).  Dahlberg and Conyers (1973) found that a single male may mate with multiple females at different times. Egg counts of 330 to 2,000 were common although nests may contain up to 9,000 eggs.  These large nests frequently contain eggs at various stages of development (2461).  The males guard and fan the eggs until they hatch in 4-5 days (Saksena and Joseph (1972).  Spawning season in Mississippi begins in April and continues through October in Mississippi and Tampa Bay (664, 2462).  High summer maximum temperatures may suppress spawning as it does for G. robustum in Tampa Bay (2470).
Fecundity: The information on fecundity is limited, but Dahlberg and Conyers (1973) found between 701 and 1,382 eggs in the ovaries of 3 naked gobies collected in Georgia.

sections.heading: Length Range
sections.content:
Egg:  The unfertilized egg of the naked goby is an opaque yellow sphere approximately 0.5 mm in diameter (2359), but may be as large as 0.72 mm (2461).  After fertilization, the elliptical egg, measuring 1.2-1.4 mm along the major axis and 0.5-0.7 mm along the minor, is demersal and attached by fibrous bundles (2359, 2321).  Eggs hatch in 4-5 days at 24 to 28 C (2321).
Larvae:  Newly hatched naked gobies are between 2.0 and 2.6 mm and have a conspicuous swim bladder (2359, 2321).  These larvae are planktonic and disperse throughout the water column (Nero 1977).  The size range of planktonic larvae is from 2 to 12 mm TL however the abundance of larvae in the water column declines rapidly above 8 mm.  Larvae above 8 mm become "demersal larvae" (2458).  Demersal larvae aggregate in shoals within 0.5 m of the substrate, usually above oyster bars, in groups of 2-3 up to several hundred individuals.  Demersal larvae range in size from 7 to 11 mm TL.  Upon collection, larger demersal larvae will settle on their pelvic fins in typical goby fashion and within a day become pigmented and indistinguishable from small juveniles (2458, 1991).  Settlement of larvae usually occurs at 9-12 mm TL (2458).
Juvenile:  After settlement, metamorphosis occurs rapidly with pigment developing in the dorsal area within 24 hrs (2459).  Juveniles may grow to 18 mm during their first summer of life (2358).
Adult:  Maturity is reached between 25 and 30 mm (2358), however males typically reach a larger size with the largest male reaching 50 mm and the largest female reaching only 37 mm (2461).  Males also tend to have darker body coloration (1915).  The sexes are distinguishable by the shape of their genital papilla with the male's being triangular and compressed while the female's is conical and fleshy (2464).

sections.heading: FOOD HABITS
sections.content: Hildebrand and Schroeder (1928) found that naked gobies in Chesapeake Bay eat Gammarus amphipods, other small crustaceans, annelids, small fish and fish eggs.

sections.heading: ECOLOGICAL INTERACTIONS
sections.content: Because it is common or abundant in estuarine and oligohaline hard bottom habitats, the naked goby is of ecological importance. It is an abundant primary and secondary consumer and prey for a variety of invertebrates and fishes (163).  Dovel (1971) and Shenker et al. (1983) found that as the numerically dominant ichthyoplankton in Chesapeake Bay, the naked goby may potentially be a valuable forage source for other fish species.  As adults they are abundant members of the oyster reef community.
